newsitem.title: UK: UK's Heseltine renews attack on Labour "con-trick".
newsitem.headline: UK's Heseltine renews attack on Labour "con-trick".

text.p: Deputy Prime Minister Michael Heseltine on Wednesday defied criticism he had gone too far in saying certain businessmen were a front for the Labour party, and renewed his attack on Labour's business policy.

Heseltine's outburst at Tuesday's launch of a report on British competitiveness dismayed many Conservative members of parliament, who saw it as a serious public relations blunder at a critical time with an election due by May.
But Heseltine shrugged off the criticism, dismissing suggestions from reporters at Wednesday's specially-convened news conference that he was in a hole and should stop digging.
"You may think we should stop digging. I think we should dig and dig deeper," said Heseltine, flanked at the news conference by Conservative party chairman Brian Mawhinney.
The row began at Tuesday's launch of the business report by a commission of businessmen and academics and sponsored by the left-leaning Institute for Public Policy Research (IPPR).

Labour leader Tony Blair, well ahead in the polls, used the launch to make a pledge, part of a series designed to rid Labour of its old anti-business, tax-and-spend image, not to scrap the free-market reforms introduced by the Conservatives.

But Heseltine demanded an invitation from the IPPR to speak after Blair and criticised the report, which largely endorsed Labour's policies, as seriously flawed and accused the businessmen of being apologists for Labour.
But his outburst angered members of the report commission.

Professor George Bain, the head of the London School of Business and chairman of the commission, said he was "flabbergasted" by Heseltine's criticism and wrote a letter to the Financial Times saying the commission had no party agenda.
But Heseltine said on Wednesday that two key members of the commission, GEC managing director George Simpson and British Aerospace chairman Bob Bauman, had not signed the letter.
"Labour tried to fake business support for Tony Blair and failed. The IPPR is nothing but a front organisation for New Labour," Heseltine said.

The deputy prime minister said others might now have to consider whether there were grounds for complaint over the IPPR's registration as a charity. Charities are not allowed to be directly involved in politics.

Heseltine also renewed his attack on the pledge by Labour economic spokesman Gordon Brown not to raise tax rates and to keep spending in check if Labour got into power, calling it a "con-trick...without one single shred of credibility".
